final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

report.markdown:
> Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard, barks at every dog on walks. South Bay CA, evenings + weekends. Prices verified 2026-08-04.

---

# 1. Hire a trainer, or do it yourself?

**Do both — but not in the way most people mean. Do the leash work yourself, and buy coaching for the reactivity. Total first spend: $300 plus ~$100 of gear.**

### The reasoning

**The pulling and the barking are the same problem, not two problems.** He is an over-aroused adolescent on a tight leash. A tight leash is not neutral — it physically amplifies reactivity: the dog can't move away, can't do a normal curving approach, feels the tension travel down the line from your hands, and the frustration comes out as barking. Fix the leash and you have already removed a large part of the trigger. That's the part you can absolutely do yourself, and it's mostly about *your* mechanics, not his.

**But the reactivity part is where DIY quietly goes wrong.** The failure mode is not lack of effort, it's working too close. People take the reactive dog on the normal walk, he barks, and every walk becomes another rehearsal of barking. Behaviour that gets rehearsed gets stronger. What you're buying with a trainer is someone telling you *how far back to stand* and *when you've moved in too fast* — the two judgement calls that are almost impossible to make on your own dog.

**Why this is a coachable case rather than a behaviour emergency:**

| Factor | Reading |
|---|---|
| Age 14 months | Adolescent peak. Reactivity that shows up here is very often frustration and arousal, not a settled temperament. Highly workable. |
| Barks at *every* dog, on leash | Classic pattern-based leash reactivity, not targeted aggression. |
| No bite history mentioned | Keeps you eligible for group classes and out of the expensive private-only bracket. |
| Border collie | Genetically wired to lock onto movement and to be bothered by things at a distance. Needs a job and a lot of sniffing, not just more exercise. |

**What tips it away from "pure DIY":** you have no way to control the other dogs on a public street, and the exact skill you need — reading his body language and bailing out *before* he goes over threshold — is the thing a coach can see and you can't.

**What tips it away from "just hire someone":** at 14 months with no bite history, spending $1,500 on private in-home sessions as the *first* move is buying more than the problem needs. The mechanics you have to learn get delivered just as well by a structured class, and the actual work happens on your walks either way. Nobody can train this dog except the person holding the leash.

### The escalation trigger — be honest about this

Move to private in-home training immediately, do not wait out the four weeks, if **any** of these happen:
- He bites, snaps, or makes contact with a dog or a person
- He redirects onto you or the leash when frustrated
- He starts barking/lunging at **people**, not just dogs
- You get physically pulled over or injured
- Four consistent weeks pass with **zero** change in the distance he can tolerate

---

# 2. If hiring — three real local options

### Recommendation: enrol in HSSV Top Dogs Level 1. $300.

| | HSSV "Top Dogs" | In Tune Dog Training | Stacy's Wag'N'Train |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Format** | Group class, online (L1) / in-person Milpitas (L2) | Private, in-home | Private, in-home + virtual |
| **Entry price** | **$300** for 6 weeks | **$195–$325** consult | **$190** consult alone |
| **Realistic total** | **$300** (or $600 through L2) | **$845–$1,400** (6 sessions) | **$1,500** (the "6-pack") |
| **Evenings?** | Yes — next cohort 6:15pm | Ask; caps at 2–3 clients/day | Ask; books 2–3 weeks out |
| **Method** | Force-free | Force-free, Fear Free certified | Force-free, since 1998 |
| **Best for** | Learning the protocol cheaply | Personalised, sliding scale available | Deepest experience, highest cost |

---

**① Humane Society Silicon Valley — "Top Dogs" reactive-dog series** ← start here
901 Ames Ave, Milpitas CA 95035 · (408) 262-2133 x352 · dogtraining@hssv.org

- **Level 1 (Reactive Dogs): $300.** Six weeks, entirely online via Zoom. First session 90 min, then five 50-min sessions. Purpose-built for leash and barrier reactivity.
- **Next cohort: starts 08/19/2026 at 6:15pm** — an evening slot, fits your constraint.
- **Level 2: $300**, in-person in Milpitas, prerequisite is L1. Real-time coaching around other reactive dogs at controlled distances. This is your step after week 4.
- **Level 3: $300**, sport-based (rally, urban parkour, tricks) with focus work around dogs — genuinely good for a collie.
- Eligibility: dog 8 months+ ✓, **no bite history** required.

*Why it wins:* $300 for six weeks of expert coaching costs about what one private session costs elsewhere. The online format means you learn the mechanics at home before you're standing in a parking lot with a barking dog on the end of a leash. And it drops you straight into an in-person progression that's exactly where a reactive dog needs to go next.

**② In Tune Dog Training** — Nancy Le, CTC, SA Pro Trainer, CSAT, Fear Free certified
nancy@intunedogtraining.com · Serves San Jose, Campbell, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Mountain View, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos.

- Initial consultation **$195–$325**; follow-ups **$130–$215**. Recommends ~6 sessions at roughly twice a month → **~$845–$1,400** all in.
- **Offers tiered pricing for households earning under $115K/year.**
- Caps at 2–3 clients per day, so evening availability is the real constraint — confirm before you commit.

**③ Stacy's Wag'N'Train** — Stacy Braslau-Schneck, CPDT-KA, San Jose since 1998
stacy@wagntrain.com · email is the practical way to reach her · books 2–3 weeks out

- Behaviour consultation alone: **$190**.
- **"Beginning Behavior Modification 6-pack": $1,500** — six 1-hr lessons, 1–2 weeks apart. This is the correct tier for reactivity.
- Note the trap: the cheaper **$800 "4-pack" is explicitly described as being for dogs *without* behaviour-modification needs**. Don't buy down into it.
- Foundation package $3,000 (14 lessons) exists for aggression/anxiety cases — overkill here.

*Backup if you want a third quote:* **D For Dogz**, force-free, Silicon Valley, offers a free intro call — but publishes no pricing, you have to ask.

---

# 3. The four-week plan

### Rules that hold for all four weeks

1. **He never gets to rehearse the barking.** Every outburst makes the behaviour stronger. If he blows up, you were too close — add distance, don't correct. A bark is information, not disobedience.
2. **Split the walks.** One 10-minute *training walk* (boring route, leash rules enforced) and a separate *sniff walk* (long line, no rules, let him sniff). Trying to do both in one outing is the single most common reason loose-leash training fails.
3. **No on-leash nose-to-nose greetings. Zero, for four weeks.** On-leash greetings are what build frustrated-greeter reactivity in the first place.
4. **Border collie tax.** Two food puzzles or scatter feeds a day plus one 10-min trick/shaping session. A dog running on a permanently high arousal baseline cannot learn anything. Adolescents also need 14–16 hours of sleep — an over-tired dog looks exactly like a reactive one.
5. **Keep a log.** One line per session: date, location, closest distance he stayed quiet at, number of outbursts. Without the number you can't tell progress from a good day — and it's the most useful thing you can hand a trainer.

**Time budget:** ~20 min/day of deliberate training plus normal walks. Setup sessions go on the weekend.

---

### Week 0 — this weekend (setup)

**Gear (~$80–100):**
- Y-front **front-clip harness** — Blue-9 Balance or 2Hounds Freedom, ~$40–50. The front attachment turns his momentum sideways instead of letting him lean into a collar.
- **6ft fixed leash**, ideally double-ended so you can clip front *and* back for steering, ~$20–30. **Not a retractable** — retractables train constant leash tension, the exact behaviour you're removing.
- Hip treat pouch ~$15. Soft high-value treats (cheese, chicken, hot dog), pea-sized. Reserve one type **exclusively** for dog-sightings.

**Find your threshold number.** Saturday morning, go somewhere with predictable dog traffic (park path, pet store lot, edge of a school field). Sit well back. Move closer in stages until he first *notices* a dog and tenses but does **not** bark. Measure that distance in paces or car-lengths and **write it down**. Every session in weeks 3 and 4 keys off this number.

**Scout two routes:** a boring low-dog-traffic street for training walks, and somewhere you can do a long-line sniff walk without meeting dogs.

---

### Week 1 — lower the baseline, build the escape hatches

*Goal: voluntary eye contact anywhere in the house and front yard, plus two reliable ways to get his attention off something.*

Daily, 2 × 5 min indoors:
- **Check-in / name game.** Every time he voluntarily looks at your face: "yes", feed. Don't ask for it — you're paying for the *offer*. Kitchen → front yard by day 5.
- **Hand target.** Flat palm, he boops it, "yes", feed. This becomes your steering wheel later.
- **"Find it" scatter.** Say "find it", toss 5–10 treats on the ground behind you. Sniffing is self-soothing and drops arousal fast. This is your emergency button in week 3.
- **U-turn / "let's go."** Say it, pivot 180°, treat at your thigh as he catches up. 10 reps a day with **no dog anywhere near**, until it's automatic *for you*.

3× this week: 20–30 min decompression sniff walk on a long line somewhere quiet. No training, no rules. Sniffing lowers arousal more than running does.

**Gate to week 2:** 8/10 marked check-ins in the front yard, and a U-turn he follows without you pulling.

---

### Week 2 — loose-leash mechanics on a boring route

*Goal: 20 consecutive slack-leash steps on the quiet street, three days running.*

**The one rule, with zero exceptions:** leash goes tight → you stop dead, feet planted, say nothing. Slack returns → you walk on. Forward motion is the only reward a pulling dog cares about, so pulling must never produce it. Expect the first two sessions to cover about 30 feet. That's normal, not failure.

- **Penalty yards.** If stopping isn't enough, calmly reverse and walk *away* from whatever he's pulling toward.
- **1-2-3 pattern game.** Walk and count aloud "1, 2, 3", treat at your side on "3", repeat continuously. Gives a collie a predictable rhythm to lock onto and keeps his head at your knee instead of scanning the horizon.
- **Reward position**, not just absence of pulling — feed at your thigh every 5–10 slack steps.

Location ladder, advance only when the current rung is easy: hallway → driveway → quiet cul-de-sac → mildly busier residential street. **Do not** take this onto the dog-traffic route yet.

**Gate to week 3:** 20 slack steps on the quiet street, three days running, U-turn still working.

---

### Week 3 — engage/disengage with other dogs, at distance, on purpose

*Goal: he sees a dog at your threshold distance and chooses to look back at you.*

**This is set-up work, not walk work.** Go to your scouted spot, park at your threshold distance, sit still. You are an observer, not a passer-by. **5–10 minutes maximum**, three times this week — two weekday evenings, one weekend morning. Quit while he's still succeeding.

- **Stage 1 (sessions 1–2):** a dog appears, he looks at it → mark **the look** ("yes") → feed. Every dog, every time. You're not asking for anything. You're building *other dog appears = chicken appears*. Don't wait for calm, don't ask for a sit.
- **Stage 2 (session 3+):** once he looks at a dog and then whips his head back to you for the treat — that's the moment. Now mark the **look back** instead, and pay bigger. He's choosing to disengage on his own.

**If a dog gets too close:** "find it" scatter behind you, or the U-turn. Both if needed. Never a correction.

**If he barks:** you were too close, full stop. Leave calmly, add 10–15 feet next time, log the new distance.

Meanwhile: keep the leash rule on the boring route, keep the sniff walks, keep avoiding dog-heavy routes on normal walks entirely.

**Gate to week 4:** three consecutive sessions at threshold with zero outbursts and visible look-backs.

---

### Week 4 — shrink the distance, merge into real walks

*Goal: pass a dog on the opposite side of a residential street without a sustained outburst, at least half the time.*

- **Shrink slowly.** Close the gap by 10–20% only after three consecutive sessions where the current distance is visibly *boring* to him. A bark at the new distance means go back and stay another week. Progress here is measured in feet, not weeks.
- **Add movement.** Static dogs are easier than moving ones. Graduate from sitting-and-watching to **parallel walking** — same direction, far across a field or wide path. If you can borrow a calm friend's dog for a parallel walk, that's the most valuable session of the whole month.
- **Merge into real walks.** When a dog appears: spot it early (scanning ahead is *your* job), create distance — cross the road, step behind a parked car, arc wide — then mark and feed as you pass. The goal is a clean **pass**, not a greeting.
- **Recheck the log.** Compare week 4's threshold distance to your week 0 number. No movement after four consistent weeks → book private training.

---

### What four weeks actually buys you

**Yes:** a leash you can hold with two fingers on a quiet street, a reliable U-turn, and a measurably larger distance at which he can see a dog and stay quiet.

**No:** a dog who ignores other dogs on a busy path. That's a 3–6 month project. Four weeks is the foundation, not the finish. Which is exactly why HSSV Level 2 exists — book it when you get there.

---

## Do this week

1. **Register for HSSV Top Dogs Level 1** — $300, cohort starts 08/19/2026 6:15pm → https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622
2. **Buy the gear** — front-clip harness, 6ft fixed leash, treat pouch, ~$100
3. **Saturday: find your threshold number** and scout your two routes
4. **Monday: start Week 1**

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid — do the leash mechanics yourself, buy coaching for the reactivity. Concretely: enrol in HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" ($300, six weeks, online, evenings) and run the 4-week home plan alongside it. Do NOT buy a $1,500 private package as your first move.

WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT CALL FOR THIS DOG
1. Two symptoms, one root. Pulling and barking-at-dogs are the same problem — an over-aroused adolescent on a tight leash. A tight leash physically amplifies reactivity (the dog is restrained, frustrated, and braced). Fixing the leash mechanics removes a large fraction of the barking on its own, and that part is genuinely DIY-able.
2. Age is in your favour. 14 months is peak adolescence. Frustration-based reactivity is extremely common at this age in under-socialised rescues and has a good prognosis. Professionals distinguish reactivity (a disproportionate over-reaction) from aggression (intent/attempt to cause harm) — barking and lunging with no bite history is the former.
3. Breed works for you. Border collies are movement-sensitive (why other dogs at distance set them off) but also unusually biddable and fast to condition. They respond very well to structured, short, high-rate-of-reinforcement sessions and to mental work before walks.
4. But reactivity is the one thing DIY reliably fails at, because it needs a decoy dog at a controlled distance. You cannot manufacture that on a neighbourhood sidewalk — random dogs appear too close, too fast, and every over-threshold blow-up sets you back. That is exactly what a reactive-dog class provides, and it is why the class beats a book.
5. Cost logic. The class pathway is $300 (L1) or $600 (L1+L2) vs ~$845–$1,500 for a private package. Start cheap; escalate only if the cheap thing plateaus.

WHAT PURE DIY WOULD COST YOU
- Money: ~$60–$110 in gear (see below). Effectively free after that.
- Time: 15–20 min/day of deliberate training plus restructured walks, for 8–12 weeks.
- Risk: the common DIY failure mode is practising at too short a distance, letting the dog rehearse barking daily, and slowly making it worse. Also the risk of buying a prong/e-collar out of frustration, which suppresses the bark while leaving (or worsening) the underlying emotion.

GEAR TO BUY BEFORE WEEK 1 (this is the DIY portion, do it regardless of the hire decision)
- Y-front front-clip harness — a front attachment point steers the dog's momentum sideways instead of letting them lean into a collar. Blue-9 Balance Harness is the commonly recommended one; a 2Hounds Freedom is the other. ~$40–$50.
- 6 ft fixed-length leash, plus ideally a double-ended leash so you can clip front AND back for steering. NO retractable leash — it trains constant tension, which is the exact opposite of what you want. ~$20–$30.
- A treat pouch that stays on your hip, and genuinely high-value soft treats (cheese, chicken, hot dog) reserved ONLY for dog-sightings. ~$15.
- Optional: a clicker or just a consistent marker word ("yes"). $3.

WHEN TO STOP DIY AND HIRE A PRIVATE PRO IMMEDIATELY (escalation triggers)
- Any bite, snap, or injury to a dog or person — this moves out of "reactivity" and out of the group-class pathway entirely (HSSV classes explicitly exclude dogs with bite history).
- Redirection: the dog bites the leash, your sleeve, or your hand mid-outburst.
- Barking/lunging at PEOPLE as well as dogs, or freezing/stiffening/hard staring rather than noisy frustration.
- Four consistent weeks of below-threshold work with no measurable increase in the distance at which the dog can stay calm.
- You cannot find any walking route where the dog stays under threshold — that means management alone is failing and you need a professional plan.

3x THIS WEEK: 20-30 min decompression sniff walk on a long line somewhere quiet. No training, no rules, let him sniff. Sniffing lowers arousal more than running does.

ENRICHMENT: two food puzzles or scatter feeds daily, one 10-min trick session.

PASS GATE to move to Week 2: 8 out of 10 marked check-ins in the front yard with mild distractions, and a U-turn he follows without you having to pull.

subtasks.title: Week 2: loose-leash mechanics on a boring route
subtasks.description:
GOAL: 20 consecutive slack-leash steps on the quiet street, three days running.

THE ONE RULE, applied with zero exceptions: leash goes tight, you stop dead, feet planted, say nothing. The moment slack returns (he looks back, steps back, whatever), you walk on. Forward motion is the only reward that matters to a pulling dog, so pulling must never produce it. Expect the first two sessions to cover about 30 feet. That's normal.

EXERCISES:
1. Penalty yards: if stopping isn't enough, calmly reverse direction and walk away from whatever he's pulling toward.
2. 1-2-3 pattern game: walk and count aloud '1, 2, 3', deliver a treat at your side on '3'. Repeat continuously. This gives a border collie a predictable rhythm to lock onto and keeps his head at your knee instead of scanning.
3. Reward position, not just absence of pulling — feed at your left thigh every 5-10 steps of slack.

LOCATION LADDER — only advance when the previous rung is easy: hallway, driveway, quiet cul-de-sac, mildly busier residential street. Do NOT take this onto the dog-traffic route yet.

SPLIT THE WALKS: 10-min training walk (rules on) and a separate sniff walk (rules off, long line). Trying to do both in one walk is why loose-leash training usually fails.

PASS GATE to move to Week 3: 20 slack-leash steps on the quiet street, three days running, plus the U-turn still works.

subtasks.title: Week 3: engage-disengage with other dogs, at distance, on purpose
subtasks.description:
GOAL: he can see another dog at your threshold distance and choose to look back at you.

THIS IS SET-UP WORK, NOT WALK WORK. Go to the spot you scouted, park at your threshold distance from the dog traffic, sit still. You are an observer, not a passer-by. 5-10 minutes MAX, three times this week — two weekday evenings and one weekend morning. Quit while he is still succeeding.

STAGE 1 (sessions 1-2): a dog appears in view. He looks at it. You mark THE LOOK ('yes') and feed. Repeat for every dog. You are not asking for anything. You are building 'other dog appears = chicken appears'. Do not wait for calm, do not ask for a sit.

STAGE 2 (session 3 onward): once he starts looking at a dog and then whipping his head back to you for the treat — that's the moment. Now mark the LOOK BACK instead, and pay bigger for it. He is now choosing to disengage on his own.

EMERGENCY TOOLS if a dog appears too close: 'find it' scatter behind you, or the U-turn. Both, if needed. Never a correction.

IF HE BARKS: you were too close, full stop. Calmly leave, add 10-15 feet next time, and write the new distance in the log. A bark is information, not disobedience.

MEANWHILE: keep enforcing the leash rule on the boring route, keep the sniff walks, keep avoiding dog-heavy routes entirely on normal walks.

PASS GATE to move to Week 4: three consecutive sessions at your threshold distance with zero outbursts and visible look-backs.

subtasks.title: Week 4: shrink the distance and merge it into real walks
subtasks.description:
GOAL: pass a dog on the opposite side of a normal residential street without a sustained outburst, at least half the time.

1. SHRINK, SLOWLY. Only close the gap by 10-20% after three consecutive sessions where the current distance is visibly boring to him. If a smaller distance produces a bark, go back out and stay there another week. Progress in this work is measured in feet, not weeks.

2. ADD MOVEMENT. Static dogs are easier than moving ones. Move from sitting-and-watching to parallel walking: you walk the same direction as a dog far across a field or a wide park path. If you can borrow a calm friend's dog for a parallel walk on the weekend, that is the single most valuable session of the whole month.

3. MERGE INTO REAL WALKS. When a dog appears on an actual walk, the sequence is: spot it early (this is your job, scan ahead constantly), create distance — cross the road, step behind a parked car, arc wide — then mark and feed as you pass. The goal is a clean PASS. Not a greeting. Still no nose-to-nose greetings.

4. RECHECK YOUR LOG. Compare week 4's threshold distance to the number you wrote down in Week 0. If it hasn't moved at all after four consistent weeks, that's the trigger to book a private trainer (see the escalation list on the DIY-vs-hire subtask).

AFTER WEEK 4: keep going. Same protocol, closing distance gradually, for another 2-5 months. This is the point where the HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 in-person class ($300) is worth booking, because you'll have real dogs at controlled distances with a trainer watching.

subtasks.title: Register for HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" reactive-dog class ($300)
subtasks.description:
The recommended first spend. $300, six weeks, entirely online via Zoom, so no logistics and no risk of a bad encounter in a parking lot. First session 90 min, then five 50-min sessions.

The cohort listed on their site starts 08/19/2026 at 6:15pm — an evening slot, which fits. Register here: https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622
Class info page: https://www.hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/

Eligibility check before you pay: dog must be 8 months+ (he's 14 months, fine) and have NO bite history toward dogs or people. If he has ever bitten, do not register — email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation instead.

If that cohort is full, email dogtraining@hssv.org or call (408) 262-2133 x352 and ask for the next Top Dogs Level 1 start date, and ask them to add you to the waitlist.

While you're on the phone, also ask: what day/time does Top Dogs Level 2 (in-person, $300, at 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas) usually run? You'll want it right after L1 and it's worth knowing now whether it lands on an evening or a weekend.

subtasks.title: Buy the gear: front-clip harness, fixed leash, treat pouch
subtasks.description:
Do this before Week 1 regardless of the trainer decision — the leash work doesn't start without it.

- Y-front front-clip harness: Blue-9 Balance Harness or 2Hounds Freedom Harness. ~$40-50. The front attachment point turns his momentum sideways instead of letting him lean into a collar.
- 6ft fixed-length leash, ideally double-ended so you can clip front AND back rings for steering. ~$20-30. Explicitly NOT a retractable — retractables teach constant leash tension, which is the exact behaviour you're trying to remove.
- Hip treat pouch, ~$15.
- High-value soft treats (cheese, chicken, hot dog), cut pea-sized. Reserve one type EXCLUSIVELY for dog-sightings — it needs to be worth more than barking.

Total ~$80-100. Available at any Petco/Pet Food Express in the South Bay, or online.

subtasks.title: Backup: email In Tune Dog Training for a private-session quote and evening availability
subtasks.description:
Only needed if the HSSV class is full, or if after four weeks the log shows no movement in threshold distance.

Nancy Le, In Tune Dog Training — nancy@intunedogtraining.com | https://www.intunedogtraining.com/book
Certified, force-free, in-home, serves San Jose + Campbell/Sunnyvale/Santa Clara/Cupertino/Mountain View/Los Gatos/Milpitas/Los Altos.

Published pricing: initial consultation $195-$325, follow-ups $130-$215; she recommends starting with 6 sessions about twice a month. Realistic total ~$845-$1,400.

Three things to ask in the email:
1. Do you have evening or weekend appointment slots? (She caps at 2-3 clients/day, so this is the real constraint.)
2. Where exactly in the $195-$325 / $130-$215 ranges does a 14-month reactive adolescent land? Get a firm number before booking.
3. You advertise tiered pricing for households under $115K — what's the process to apply? (Only relevant if that applies to you.)

Alternative if you'd rather pay for the most experienced person in the South Bay: Stacy's Wag'N'Train, stacy@wagntrain.com, training in San Jose since 1998. Her "Beginning Behavior Modification 6-pack" is $1,500 (the $800 4-pack is explicitly NOT for behaviour-modification cases, so don't be tempted by the cheaper tier). Standalone behaviour consult is $190. Email is the only way to reach her.

subtasks.title: Set a Week-4 review: compare threshold distance to the Week 0 number
subtasks.description:
Put a reminder in your calendar for four weeks after you start.

Open the training log and compare the closest distance he could stay quiet at in Week 0 against the same number at the end of Week 4.

- Distance shrank meaningfully → it's working. Keep going, and book HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 in-person ($300) for the next stage.
- Distance unchanged after four consistent weeks → that's the escalation trigger. Book private in-home sessions (In Tune, or Stacy's Wag'N'Train).
- Any bite, snap, redirection onto your arm or the leash, or barking/lunging at people rather than just dogs → escalate immediately, don't wait for week 4. That's outside the group-class pathway and outside DIY.
